# Glenmore, and the 15th of January

Some of you have been hearing about this in bits and pieces for a few weeks now, and some of you heard it from somebody else before I had the chance to say it to you properly. I know that. I'm sorry for that.

It is easier to let a thing travel on its own than to sit down and say it out loud, and then to be surprised when it turns up somewhere you didn't expect it to. That's what happened. So I'm going to put all of it here, once, in one place, and there's a date near the end of this you can all write down and look at, because I would rather every one of you heard this from me than from a cousin on a WhatsApp group.

The short version, so you don't have to read to the bottom for the headline: **we have sold the house at Glenmore.** The sale was agreed on 3 November. **It closes on Friday the 15th of January 2027.** Please put that in your diary now, while it's only one date and one thing.

After that, I'll explain why, and what happens to the house and to the things in it, and I'll say the harder bits as well. There are a couple of things in here I've not said out loud to anybody yet, including one of them to Declan, and by the time you've finished you may want to ring me, which is entirely fine.

---

## The house

Glenmore was built in 1931 by Pádraig Mulkerrin, Tom's grandfather, on land his father had, and Tom grew up in it and then brought me into it, and it has been the Mulkerrin house for three generations and the family house for two of us after that. There isn't a lot to say about it that hasn't already been said in this family at one time or another. You all know the hallway with the flagstones, the range in the kitchen that took an hour and a half to heat, the way the back door would stick in a wet February and then decide to stick in the dry ones too, for spite. You know the haggard at the bottom and the field above it and the lake further down the lane, and the gorse, and the bit of the road where the heather comes right up to the gate.

It's a good house. It was a good house. It was also, by the end, a house that wanted a great deal of money put into it, and I want to be honest about that, because I don't want anybody thinking I've let go of something perfect. It wasn't perfect. It hasn't been for a long time.

Ó Flaithearta's did a roof survey in September. The slates want doing and the back chimney wants doing, and the quote came to €38,000. There's damp in the back bedroom — the one at the end with the view of the lake — which has never entirely gone away and which the surveyor has described, in his careful way, as persistent. And the septic tank has to be replaced, because it has to be replaced to sell to anybody at all, not just to us. So the sale was never going to be a case of signing a bit of paper and pocketing the difference. It was always going to be money going out before money came in.

I've been driving out to Glenmore every fortnight since Tom died in March 2024, to air the house and check the pipes. It's forty minutes each way. People say that sounds like a lot and it is a lot. There was a stretch in the first year when I could have told you what was happening under that roof without being there.

---

## The buyers, and the price

The people buying it are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin's from Maam Cross. They have two small children. They want to live in it — to actually live in it, all year, with their children growing up in it. That was the thing I wanted. Not a holiday let, not a place with the good bits kept and the rest shut up. A house with children in it.

The Dublin crowd offered more over the summer. Quite a lot more. I took the lower one, and I took the lower one on purpose, and I'd do it again. I grew up in a house like this, so I know exactly what it does to a family when it sits empty. I know what it did to this one. I'd rather the money went to people who'll put their boots on the floorboards in the hall and let them get muddy, and I'd rather I didn't spend two years feeling bad about it.

---

## Why now

I made up my mind over the best part of two years, and I want to say that because I don't think this was a decision I took in a bad afternoon and have been regretting since. It came slowly and then all at once.

Part of it is practical. The house needed spending on, and it needed spending before it could be sold, and every month I put off was a month of the same forty-minute drive and the same Sunday feeling that I should be doing something about it. Part of it is that I have been alone in that house since March 2024, and I have discovered something about myself that I didn't know and wouldn't have guessed.

Last February I went out to the house in the frost and slipped on the step at the back door. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get myself up. Twenty minutes. And the thing that stayed with me was not the cold or the fall — it was that nobody knew. I didn't tell anybody, and I didn't ring anybody, and I lay there and did the arithmetic of who I was going to ring and what I was going to say, and then I got up and locked the door and drove home and told nobody about it. I've only mentioned it here because it's the reason for the rest of it, and because it's the sort of thing I would sit on and sit on.

I have been afraid of that house since the fall. Not of anything in it. Of being in it on my own. And I cannot go on maintaining it. Not honestly, not for much longer. I'm seventy-one. I did the maths on what the next ten years of that would look like and I didn't like any of it.

I know some of you think I should have waited until Declan came over in the summer. I have thought about that a great deal. I don't regret the decision to sell. I do regret not sitting down with him first and talking it through, and I'll come back to that, because it's a different thing and I don't want to blur the two together.

---

## What stays

We're keeping the things that matter and the things that are actually ours. The dresser goes to Úna's. Pádraig's fiddle — the fiddle, not a copy of it — is coming with us, and there's a lesson booked in the spring, because it's been silent in a case for thirty years and it deserves better than that. The photographs stay, all of them, in the albums and in the boxes, and I am having the negatives copied and the albums scanned, and I'll send each of you a copy, so you can all argue for yourselves about which one of Tom as a baby is the worst photograph ever taken.

The Sacred Heart lamp stays on its shelf. The gate sign stays at the gate, or rather — the Joyces have agreed it can stay at the gate, and I was quietly pleased about that, more than I expected to be.

And the Joyces have said something that I want you all to know: the family can come out and walk the land any time. Any time. Not by appointment, not on the day. Walk the lane, walk the haggard, walk down to the lake if you want to. That's the arrangement, and it's a generous one, and I intend to take them up on it often.

---

## Sunday the 13th of December — come out to the house

Before it's cleared, before the furniture goes and the curtains come down and the rooms stop being rooms, I want us all to come out to Glenmore one more time. All of you. Anyone who can.

**Sunday the 13th of December. Soup and sandwiches at one o'clock. Bring wellies.**

There'll be tea, and there'll be children welcome, and there'll be no ceremony of any kind, because Tom would have found that unbearable. Bring your own layers. Bring a torch if you want to go down to the lake, which you will want to, and mind the grass on the slope down is slippy after rain. If you're coming from abroad and it's too far for a day, come for the week before if you can and we'll put you on.

If you can't make the 13th, come another day. There's no deadline on this except the one in January.

---

## Declan

This is the part I've been dreading writing, so I'm going to write it straight.

Declan heard about the sale from Gráinne on a WhatsApp, not from me. Gráinne was passing on what she'd been told and she had no way of knowing what she was about to do, and that is not a criticism of her and I wouldn't want anyone to make it one. But it wasn't right, and the not-right of it was mine.

He rang me at two in the morning his time. I don't know what time it was here and it didn't matter. He said I was selling Dad. And I said things back that I shouldn't have said. Some of them fair enough and some of them not, and I've been turning them over since, and the ones that weren't fair enough I would like to take back, and I'm not going to pretend they didn't happen or that they didn't land.

Here's what I want to say to him, and I'll put it here because I think he'd rather read it than have to ask for it.

**I'm sorry you heard it that way. I'm not sorry for the decision.** Those are two separate things and I've kept them separate on purpose.

I have never been angry with Declan. Not once, in all of this, and I want that on the record, and I want it on the record in a place where he will actually read it, because I know he has been reading this blog quietly and I don't think I've said what I should have said for some time now.

You were the first person I wanted to tell and I didn't tell you, and I don't have a good enough reason for that. I told myself it was because I didn't want to say it over the phone, and there was some truth in that, but there was more truth in the fact that I knew what you'd say. And I didn't want to hear it. That's on me, and it's a thing about me that I didn't much like discovering.

The door is open. Not in a month, not in the summer. Now. If you want to ring me, ring me. If you want to come out to the house, come out to the house. If you want to see the haggard, I'll walk you down to it and I'll tell you about the afternoon you wouldn't come out of the lake until your lips were blue, which you did every single summer until you were about nine, and which I have never once failed to mention since.

---

## Tom

He proposed to me in the haggard behind that house in 1979, in the rain, with the cattle watching, as if they were all in on it. I said yes before he'd finished, and he laughed at me for the rest of my life about how fast I'd said it. There was nothing romantic about the haggard in April — it was wet, it was cold, and I was soaked through before he'd got the ring out. But he chose that spot, over the table, over the good evening, and he chose it because it was the field he'd been brought up in and it was the house he wanted to hand on.

We had the good years and we had the hard years and the house stood through all of it. The children learned to swim in the lake below the house. Declan wouldn't come out until his lips were blue. There are photographs of all of that and there will be more of it in these albums than I can say in a blog post, and if you want to come and look at them, they are in the boxes in the hall and you are welcome to come and look at them.

And Tom always said the house should have children in it. Not a museum. He said it to me more than once, and the last time was not long before he died, and he was not being sentimental, he was being practical — he knew what a house does to people when it's kept like a shrine. He wanted it lived in. He wanted it loud.

So when I sat in the kitchen at Glenmore with the surveyor's quote and the septic tank bill and the whole business of it in front of me, the thing that settled it for me, more than the money and more than the winter and more than the fear of the frost on the step, was that. He would have been mightily annoyed with me for turning his house into a monument to him. That was the opposite of what he wanted.

I have come to realise, over the best part of two years, that I can keep Tom's memory without keeping the house. I can keep the fiddle and the photographs and the lamp and the gate sign and about nine hundred stories that nobody else alive can tell the way I can tell them. The house is a house. It was a good house and it should be a good house for somebody else now, with children running up the lane and the gorse getting into everything, as it always did.

---

## The date, one more time

**Friday the 15th of January 2027.**

That's when it closes. If you hear anything else about this before then — a rumour, a cousin's guess, something on a WhatsApp — ring one of us and we'll tell you straight. There is nothing hidden behind it. The price was fair. The house needed work and the work has been done. The people buying it are decent and they will look after it.

If you can, come to the house on the 13th of December. Soup, sandwiches, wellies, children, and whatever you want to say about it. Bring the photographs you want copied and I'll do them. Bring your questions. Bring your complaints. I'd rather have this conversation in the kitchen at Glenmore with a cup of tea in my hand than have it in pieces on the phone over the next three months.

I'm sorry for the way some of you found out. I'm not sorry for the decision. And I'm not going anywhere, and neither is the family — that's the thing about this that none of us has said out loud yet, and I think it's true.

I'd like to see you all in December.

— Máire

---

*If you're coming on the 13th, it'd help if you could let Úna know roughly how many you'll be, so we don't run out of soup at one o'clock. There's a lane and a rough patch at the bottom near the gate — park on the road if your car is low.*

reasons: The closing section says 'the work has been done', but the request says the roof and septic tank still need work, so the piece contradicts the supplied facts (and its own earlier text).
It does not explicitly say she is unwilling to wait until Declan’s summer visit.
